sentences.text: Septencoracias is an extinct bird related to modern rollers and other members of the order Coraciiformes.
This small bird measured approximately 25 cm in length, a size similar to a Northern carmine bee-eater.
Its skull was large relative to its body, measuring about twice the length of its humerus.
The animal possessed a stout, slightly curved beak with an upper ridge that curved gradually toward the tip, similar to modern rollers.
Distinct from the elongated, slit-like, or triangular nares found in its relatives, Septencoracias had small, egg-shaped nasal openings.
The single known fossil specimen lacks the sternum and most of the shoulder girdle, except for a left scapula that was not bifurcated like in later rollers.
It retained a small claw on its alular digit, a feature usually absent in modern birds but shared with its relative Primobucco.
Septencoracias had a very wide pelvis and hind limb proportions similar to those of modern rollers.
It is uncertain whether Septencoracias exhibited syndactyly, the fusion of toes three and four, a condition common in modern Coraciiformes.
Fossil remains of Septencoracias show soft tissue preservation, primarily within the thoracic and abdominal cavities.
Fish remains, specifically argentinoids about 10 cm long, were found in the gut of the Septencoracias specimen.
The genus Septencoracias was described by Bourdon and colleagues in 2016.
The genus contains two species: the type species Septencoracias morsensis described in 2016 and S. simillimus named in 2024.
The type specimen was discovered in the Moclay Pit on the Island of Mors in Jutland, Denmark.
The genus name Septencoracias combines 'septentrio', meaning north, with the name of modern rollers, Coracias.
The specific name morsensis refers to the Island of Mors where the fossil was found.
An additional specimen from the Tielt Formation in Belgium was tentatively identified as Septencoracias in 2019.
The presence of fish in its gut suggests early Coraciiformes had a more varied diet than modern species, which mostly eat insects and small land vertebrates.
Septencoracias is the oldest known member of the Coraciiformes, indicating the group was already diversified by the Early Eocene.
Phylogenetic analysis in 2016 identified Septencoracias as the sister taxon of Primobucco.
Fossils of Septencoracias date to the Ypresian stage of the Early Eocene, approximately 54 million years ago.
Septencoracias fossils are from the Eastern Hemisphere, the region where all modern rollers currently live.
The discovery of Septencoracias in Denmark suggests that early Coraciiformes had a much wider range in the Northern Hemisphere during the warm Eocene climate.
The time range for Septencoracias is estimated from 56 to 48.07 million years ago.
